_**User (2026-08-04 16:15:27Z)**_

can u create a little table of before and after planning stuff

---

_**Agent (2026-08-04 16:15:27Z)**_

| Planning area | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Team setup | Planner, provider, model and children required several separate choices | One execution-team choice establishes the planner, model and child roles; advanced overrides remain available |
| Source | Planning could describe a different or mutable source tree | The source is resolved first, summarized from a bounded dossier, then frozen for the Job |
| Goal shape | A short model call could fail before selecting single, review, plan or campaign | A bounded planner recommends the shape; if it is unavailable and cleanup is proven, DeadReckon can use a deterministic recommendation |
| Definition of done | Draft, critic and redraft had short or fragmented time slices | They share one 20-minute automated-work clock and each receives all remaining time |
| Provider/model | Admission could use a configured alias or a different default from the selected execution team | Planning and done authoring use the resolved provider and model selected for the launch |
| Codex output | Invalid strict schemas and obsolete feature switches could stop `start` | Schemas are validated locally and only supported Codex capabilities are requested |
| Failure recovery | An authoring failure effectively sent the operator back to the beginning | Source, launch shape, provider and model are retained; the operator can retry, revise or cancel |
| Supervisor setup | Service mutation could happen before planning and contract approval | Installation/repair is deferred until the contract and final launch are approved |
| Execution budget | Phase-local clocks and divided child allowances could starve large plans | The approved Job gets one cumulative active-work allowance—10 hours by default—and every child and completion phase inherits its remainder |
| Parallel work | Child durations could be summed and mistaken for elapsed Job time | Elapsed Job time follows the real clock; summed parallel effort is shown separately as worker-seconds |

_**Agent (2026-08-04 16:15:27Z)**_

We are close in implementation terms, but not yet at the point where I would tag it.

Current release state:

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| Version metadata | Ready: Rust, lockfile, npm wrapper and pins all say `0.8.1` |
| Real-provider proof | Previously passed for Claude Code and Codex at `0.8.1` |
| Timing/start fixes | Implemented; 32 commits have landed since the original `0.8.1` preparation |
| Release-plan workflow | Passing on every recent push |
| Main CI | Not green yet |
| `v0.8.1` tag/release | Does not exist locally, remotely, or on GitHub |
| Final install/start proof | Still pending |
| RC rehearsal | Still pending |

The remaining path is:

1. Finish and test the reboot-resume correction currently in progress.
2. Commit and push the two CI fixture fixes plus that correction.
3. Get a fresh `main` CI run fully green.
4. Fold the new timing work currently under “Unreleased” into the `0.8.1` release notes and refresh the provider proof against the final binary.
5. Install that exact binary and prove an analogous `start` reaches real execution.
6. Cut and verify a `v0.8.1-rc.N`, then—after explicit tag approval—cut and verify `v0.8.1`.

So: one focused production defect and roughly five release gates remain. This is closer to “final hardening and release rehearsal” than “more feature development,” but it is not a minutes-away tag. I would call it roughly 80% of the way to a defensible stable release.

_**Agent (2026-08-04 16:15:27Z)**_

I’m grouping the overnight failures by root cause rather than counting each red run separately. Because every push launches another full CI run, the same unresolved regression can make many successive commits look independently broken even when they share one cause.

_**Agent (2026-08-04 16:15:27Z)**_

They did not all fail for one mysterious reason. Since 04:00 UTC there were 28 failed CI runs, 5 cancelled runs, and 1 fully successful run (`c28da8`). The separate release-planning workflow has continued to pass.

The main reason the history looks so bad is that we pushed commits faster than the 15–20 minute full suite could finish. Several new commits were already queued while an older run was still discovering failures, so the same defect appears red across many later commits.

The failures came in waves:

| Wave | Cause |
|---|---|
| Early admission work | Formatting drift, a fake Codex test trying to write through the new read-only sandbox, outdated generated schemas, and tests still expecting the old deadline/lease behavior |
| Midway | Public API baseline drift, a documentation coherence assertion, and an over-broad seam test that rejected the new timing environment |
| Latest runs | One Linux timing assertion expected the entire cutoff plus cleanup to finish in under 2 seconds, even though cleanup legitimately has a 2-second grace |
| Latest runs | Supervisor production moved from checkpoint schema 2 to 3, while the shared integration fixture still waited for schema 2; this caused four tests in two suites to time out despite a healthy v3 supervisor |

The latest two CI runs are therefore failing only three test targets:

- the overly tight cleanup timing test;
- `watchkeeper_restart_boundary`, through the stale v2 fixture;
- `watchkeeper_trust_boundary`, through the same stale v2 fixture.

Those fixes are already in the working tree and pass the previously failing focused trust tests. Once the fixture was unblocked locally, it exposed one genuine reboot-resume issue: DeadReckon could resume the same logical attempt but then mistakenly spend another retry. The production correction is in place; the test is now being adjusted to simulate a real reboot by actually removing the pre-reboot process.

So the red history is mostly an integration discipline problem—rapid phased pushes plus slow full CI—not 28 independent product failures. I am now holding the next push until the combined supervisor/restart fixes pass locally, then we will trigger one meaningful fresh CI run instead of another chain of knowingly stale runs.

_**Agent (gpt-5.6-sol 2026-08-04 16:21:27Z)**_

Diagnosis: this was a DeadReckon evidence-binding regression, not a Claude failure, timeout, bad contract, or budget problem.

Causal chain:

1. `release/preflight-real.sh:82-103` created a valid exact-output contract.
2. The Claude worker completed normally, changed `purpose.sh`, and exited successfully.
3. The signed deterministic gate passed the shell check.
4. The independent Claude semantic judge completed in 16.7 seconds and returned a valid `achieved` judgment with input digest `sha256:ec352…`.
5. DeadReckon then recomputed a different evidence packet while sealing the receipt and correctly refused to issue it.
6. The supervisor consequently projected `needs_review / semantic_unavailable`.

The mismatch was introduced by commit `69a5099`:

- Before it, an ordinary leaf run used the turn-snapshot evidence baseline.
- That commit changed the judge invocation to `run_semantic_judge_against_source_with_deadline_and_cancellation(..., &state.cwd, ...)` at [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:5160).
- Receipt sealing still called snapshot-based `validate_semantic_judgment_input` at [turn_loop.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/turn_loop.rs:5311).
- The two alternatives are selected at [semantic_judge.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-runtime/src/semantic_judge.rs:226): source-tree diff versus `turn-0 → current-turn` snapshot diff.

They differ concretely in the preserved run:

- The original source tree has no `implementation-notes.html`.
- DeadReckon initialized that file before taking `turn-0`.
- Therefore the judge’s source-tree packet describes it as an added file.
- The sealing packet describes it as a modified file.
- Different unified diffs produce different evidence hashes even though the result never changed.

This can affect normal single-leaf jobs broadly because initializing and updating `implementation-notes.html` is the default workflow.

Classification:

| Layer | Finding |
|---|---|
| Product | Defect: judge and sealer use different evidence baselines. |
| Claude | Healthy: worker and semantic judge both completed successfully. |
| Contract | Healthy: the contained deterministic check passed. |
| Timing/budget | Not involved: approximately 56 seconds used from a 10-hour allowance. |
| Integrity policy | Correct: it failed closed instead of issuing an inconsistent receipt. |
| Operator reporting | Imprecise: `semantic_unavailable` hides that the judge actually achieved and receipt binding failed. |

The safest fix is to add an exact-deadline/cancellation semantic-judge entry point for ordinary leaf runs that retains the snapshot baseline, then keep snapshot validation during sealing. `diff_working_trees` explicitly documents that source-tree baselines are for composed graph results, while ordinary runs use snapshots at [artifacts.rs](/Users/gdc/deadreckon/crates/deadreckon-core/src/artifacts.rs:257).

If source-tree evidence is retained instead, the sealer must use the same source baseline—and that source must be bound to the frozen `source_tree_sha256`, not the live mutable `state.cwd`.

Verification should require:

- A regression test reproducing the absent-in-source but initialized-in-turn-0 notes file.
- A happy-path test proving one identical evidence digest is used by judge and sealer and a receipt is issued.
- Existing stale-judgment tests remaining green.
- A composed-graph test retaining its approved-source behavior.
- Rebuilding the release binary and rerunning:

```sh
DEADRECKON_BIN=/path/to/fixed/deadreckon \
PREFLIGHT_JOB_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=1200 \
release/preflight-real.sh cli:claude-code
```

That proof must reach `verified`, produce the combined receipt, deliver via `finish`, and complete the cancellation/reaping phase. I made no edits.
